title.rendered: Monthly Cost of Old Age Homes in Pune – What You Should Know Before Choosing

content.rendered:
As our loved ones grow older, ensuring their comfort, care, and happiness becomes a top priority. For many families, choosing an old age home is not just about finding a place to stay—it’s about finding a safe, nurturing environment where seniors can live with dignity, companionship, and medical support. One of the most common questions families ask is: “What is the monthly cost of an old age home in Pune?” The answer depends on several factors, including the type of care provided, location, and available facilities.

1. Understanding the Basic Cost Structure

The monthly cost of old age homes in Pune generally ranges between ₹15,000 to ₹60,000 per month, depending on the level of services and amenities offered. Basic facilities include accommodation, meals, housekeeping, and recreational activities. More premium homes, on the other hand, provide additional medical supervision, physiotherapy, and wellness programs—all of which can influence the monthly charges.

2. Type of Accommodation

Old age homes typically offer different types of rooms—shared rooms, semi-private, and private rooms.

  • Shared rooms are the most affordable option, suitable for seniors who enjoy social interaction.
  • Private rooms offer more privacy and personalized care but come at a higher monthly cost.
    The accommodation type you choose plays a significant role in determining the overall expenses.

3. Medical and Nursing Care

Some seniors require regular medical attention, while others need only minimal supervision.

  • Homes with 24×7 nursing staff, on-site doctors, and emergency care facilities will have higher monthly fees.
  • For seniors with chronic illnesses or mobility challenges, specialized care homes are available, though at an additional cost.

It’s important to evaluate the medical infrastructure of the facility before finalizing, especially if health concerns are a priority.

4. Amenities and Lifestyle Facilities

Modern old age homes in Pune are designed to provide more than just shelter. They offer a comfortable and engaging lifestyle.
Common amenities may include:

  • Nutritious meals prepared by in-house chefs
  • Fitness and wellness programs
  • Cultural and recreational activities
  • Library and meditation rooms
  • Gardens and walking tracks

Naturally, the more amenities included, the higher the monthly charges—but also the better the quality of life for residents.

5. Location and Reputation

Location is another factor influencing the cost. Homes situated in central Pune or prime areas like Kothrud, Baner, or Aundh tend to have higher rates compared to those in the outskirts. Additionally, reputed care homes with experienced staff and established credibility may charge more, but they also ensure peace of mind for families.

6. Additional Expenses to Consider

Apart from the monthly fee, there may be additional or optional costs such as:

  • Security deposit or admission fees
  • Medical check-ups and personal medications
  • Outings, events, or special celebrations
    Understanding these beforehand helps in planning the overall budget without surprises.

7. Choosing the Right Home for Your Loved One

The decision should not be based solely on cost but on the value of care. Visit the facility, speak to staff, and observe the environment. A good old age home should offer emotional comfort, safety, and medical support—all essential for senior well-being.

Conclusion

Selecting the right old age home is one of the most important decisions you’ll make for your loved one. While costs vary, the key is finding a place that offers compassionate care, comfort, and security within your budget.

title.rendered: Nursing Homes vs. Assisted Living: What’s the Difference?

content.rendered:
As our loved ones age, their care needs evolve. Families often find themselves choosing between two common senior care options — nursing homes and assisted living facilities. While both offer essential services for older adults, they cater to different levels of care, independence, and medical support. Understanding these differences is key to making the right decision for your aging family member.

Understanding Assisted Living

Assisted living is ideal for seniors who are still relatively independent but need help with daily activities like bathing, dressing, medication reminders, or mobility. These facilities provide:

  • Private or semi-private apartments
  • Meals and housekeeping services
  • Personal care assistance
  • Recreational and social activities
  • 24/7 support staff for non-medical needs

Assisted living aims to balance support with independence, allowing residents to maintain their autonomy while receiving the help they need in a safe and social environment.

Understanding Nursing Homes

Nursing homes, also known as skilled nursing facilities, are better suited for seniors who require constant medical care and supervision. These are appropriate for elderly individuals with chronic illnesses, recovering from surgery, or those with advanced mobility limitations. Services typically include:

  • Round-the-clock medical supervision by licensed nurses
  • Administration of medications and therapies
  • Rehabilitation services (physical, occupational, or speech therapy)
  • Assistance with all daily living activities
  • On-site medical equipment and support for complex conditions

Nursing homes focus more on medical care and provide a structured, clinical environment to ensure residents’ health and well-being are consistently monitored.

Key Differences at a Glance

Which One is Right for Your Loved One?

The right choice depends on your loved one’s current health, level of independence, and the kind of care they require. If they simply need help with basic tasks and enjoy social interaction, assisted living may be ideal. However, if they require skilled nursing care or have medical conditions that need constant supervision, a nursing home is the safer and more appropriate option.

Conclusion

When it comes to senior care, the goal is always to provide comfort, dignity, and the right level of support. title.rendered: Care for Dementia Patients at Home – A Guide by Swarnvihar Old Age Homes

content.rendered:
Caring for a loved one with dementia can be both emotionally rewarding and physically challenging. As the condition progresses, everyday activities become more complex, and the need for personalized support increases. At Swarnvihar Old Age Homes, we understand how important it is to provide compassionate, effective, and safe care for dementia patients at home. This blog will guide you through essential tips and strategies to ensure your loved one’s well-being while easing the burden of caregiving.

Understanding Dementia: The First Step

Dementia is a broad term for a deterioration in mental capacity that is severe enough to interfere with day-to-day functioning rather than a specific disease. The most frequent cause of dementia is Alzheimer’s disease. Memory loss, disorientation, communication problems, and personality changes are some of the symptoms. To provide the appropriate amount of help at home, it is essential to comprehend the kind and stage of dementia your loved one is suffering from.

1. Create a Safe and Supportive Environment

For those with dementia, safety at home is of utmost importance. Accidents can be avoided by making small adjustments such reducing trip hazards, locking up dangerous materials, and putting grab bars in the restroom. To reduce confusion, name rooms and objects and keep everyday items in the same locations.

2. Establish a Routine

Patients with dementia benefit greatly from structure. Establishing a regular schedule including activities, relaxation, medication, and food might help people feel less anxious and more secure. To create a feeling of familiarity, try to stick to the same routine each day.

3. Engage in Stimulating Activities

Activities that are mentally and physically engaging help maintain cognitive function and emotional well-being. Depending on their stage of dementia, consider:

  • Puzzles and memory games
  • Listening to music or singing
  • Simple gardening or household tasks
  • Art and craft activities

Always tailor activities to the individual’s abilities and interests.

4. Focus on Communication

The capacity to communicate ideas and comprehend others is impacted by dementia. Make eye contact and speak in short, straightforward phrases. Do not correct or argue; instead, be patient. As dementia worsens, nonverbal clues like touch, speech inflection, and facial expressions become increasingly significant.

5. Prioritize Nutrition and Hydration

Drinking enough water and eating a balanced diet are essential. If necessary, serve wholesome meals in smaller portions and keep an eye out for swallowing issues. Smoothies and finger snacks might be useful substitutes.

6. Take Care of the Caregiver

It can be emotionally taxing to care for someone who has dementia. It is critical to connect with support groups, seek for assistance, and take regular pauses. Keep in mind that the quality of care is directly impacted by your well-being.

7. Seek Professional Support When Needed

Sometimes, home care alone may not be enough. Swarnvihar Old Age Homes offers dementia care services that provide professional support in a homely environment. Our trained caregivers ensure the safety, dignity, and comfort of every resident while giving family members peace of mind.

Conclusion

Providing care for dementia patients at home requires empathy, patience, and continuous learning. With the right environment and support, your loved one can live with dignity and joy. At Swarnvihar Old Age Homes, we’re committed to guiding families through every step of the caregiving journey. If you need help, we’re just a call away.

title.rendered: What is the Difference Between Palliative Care and Hospice?

content.rendered:
When it comes to caring for aging loved ones, it is important to understand the various care options available. Terms like “palliative care” and “hospice” are often used interchangeably, but they serve distinct purposes. At Swarnavihar Old Age Home, we recognize the importance of clarity when making such critical decisions. Let us guide you through the differences between hospice and palliative care to help you make an informed choice.

Understanding Palliative Care

Palliative consideration is a specific type of clinical consideration that spotlights on working on the personal satisfaction for people experiencing difficult sicknesses. The essential objective of palliative consideration is to reduce torment and oversee side effects, permitting patients to live as easily as could really be expected. This sort of care isn’t restricted to end-of-life circumstances and can be given close by healing medicines.

Key Features of Palliative Care:

  • Focus on Quality of Life: Palliative care addresses physical, emotional, and psychological challenges associated with serious illnesses.
  • Holistic Approach: It involves a team of healthcare professionals, including doctors, nurses, social workers, and counselors.
  • Eligibility: Patients at any stage of a chronic or life-threatening illness can receive palliative care.
  • Setting: Palliative care can be provided in hospitals, nursing homes, or even at home.

Understanding Hospice Care

Hospice care is a particular sort of palliative consideration intended for people who are approaching the finish of life. Hospice centers around solace instead of fix and supports patients and their families during the last phases of a terminal disease. The accentuation is on poise, harmony, and profound prosperity.

title.rendered: How Can Senior Citizens Improve Their Health? | Swarnavihar Oldage Homes

content.rendered:
As we age, maintaining good health becomes increasingly important. For senior citizens, adopting healthy habits can significantly improve the quality of life, enhance physical well-being, and keep the mind sharp. At Swarnavihar Oldage Homes, we believe in promoting holistic health for seniors through a combination of physical, mental, and emotional well-being practices.

Here are some key ways senior citizens can improve their health:

1. Stay Physically Active

Regular exercise is vital for maintaining strength, flexibility, and balance as we age. Even light physical activity can reduce the risk of chronic diseases, improve mobility, and boost mood.

  • Walking:

    A simple but effective way to stay active. Seniors can take regular walks around the garden or participate in group walking sessions.

  • Yoga:

    Gentle yoga exercises are ideal for improving flexibility, balance, and mindfulness.

  • Strength Training:

    Using light weights or resistance bands can help seniors maintain muscle mass and improve bone density.

  • Swimming:

    For those with joint pain, swimming provides a low-impact way to stay active.

2. Follow a Balanced Diet

Nutrition plays a crucial role in maintaining overall health, particularly for seniors. A well-balanced diet can help manage weight, boost immunity, and reduce the risk of diseases such as diabetes, heart conditions, and high blood pressure.

  • Eat Fresh Fruits and Vegetables:

    A diet rich in colorful fruits and vegetables provides essential vitamins, minerals, and antioxidants.

  • Include Lean Proteins:

    Proteins like fish, chicken, eggs, and legumes help maintain muscle mass and support overall bodily functions.

  • Stay Hydrated:

    Drinking enough water is essential for digestion, energy levels, and cognitive function. Seniors should aim to drink at least 6-8 glasses of water per day.

  • Limit Sugar and Salt Intake:

    Reducing sugar and salt can help manage blood pressure and prevent heart-related diseases.

3. Stay Mentally Active

Cognitive health is just as important as physical health. Keeping the brain engaged helps to ward off memory loss, dementia, and other age-related cognitive decline.

  • Engage in Puzzles and Games:

    Solving crosswords, Sudoku, or playing board games like chess can help stimulate the brain and improve memory.

  • Reading:

    Whether it’s books, newspapers, or online articles, reading keeps the brain active and engaged

  • Learn a New Skill:

    Senior citizens can explore new hobbies like knitting, painting, or playing a musical instrument to keep their minds sharp.

4. Socialize Regularly

Loneliness and isolation can negatively affect mental and emotional health, especially for older adults. Socializing is essential for mental well-being and can reduce the risk of depression.

  • Participate in Group Activities:

    Group activities like dancing, singing, or attending cultural events allow seniors to connect with others and foster a sense of community.

  • Join Social Clubs:

    At Swarnavihar Oldage Homes, residents have the opportunity to join clubs where they can share interests and hobbies with others.

  • Stay Connected with Family:

    Regular visits or phone calls with family members help seniors feel loved and supported, reducing feelings of loneliness.

5. Prioritize Mental Health

Mental health is an essential aspect of overall well-being. Seniors should make mental health a priority by seeking emotional support and engaging in activities that promote happiness and relaxation.

  • Meditation and Relaxation:

    Practicing mindfulness and meditation can help manage stress, anxiety, and depression, providing mental peace and clarity.

  • Counseling and Therapy:

    Accessing professional counseling can offer emotional support and help seniors deal with life transitions.

  • Journaling:

    Writing down thoughts and feelings can be a therapeutic way to process emotions and reflect on positive life experiences.

6. Get Regular Health Checkups

Preventative care is key to maintaining good health in old age. Regular health checkups allow for early detection of potential health issues and ensure that chronic conditions are well-managed.

  • Monitor Blood Pressure and Sugar Levels:

    Regular monitoring helps manage conditions like hypertension and diabetes.

  • Routine Screenings:

    Tests like bone density scans, cholesterol checks, and cancer screenings are vital to detect health concerns early.

  • Eye and Hearing Exams:

    Vision and hearing tend to decline with age, so regular checkups are essential for maintaining sensory health.

7. Get Enough Sleep

Quality sleep is essential for physical and mental health, yet many seniors struggle with sleep disturbances. Sleep helps the body repair and recharge, improves memory, and enhances mood.

  • Maintain a Consistent Sleep Routine:

    Going to bed and waking up at the same time each day can help regulate sleep patterns.

  • Create a Relaxing Sleep Environment:

    A comfortable, quiet, and dark environment can promote better sleep quality.

  • Limit Screen Time Before Bed:

    Avoiding TV and mobile devices before bed helps the mind relax and prepares the body for restful sleep.

8. Stay Safe and Prevent Falls

Falls are a significant concern for seniors as they can lead to serious injuries. Taking steps to prevent falls can enhance safety and independence.

  • Use Assistive Devices:

    Canes, walkers, and grab bars in the bathroom can help reduce the risk of falling.

  • Wear Proper Footwear:

    Supportive, non-slip shoes can prevent accidents

  • Keep Living Spaces Safe:

    Clear pathways, remove tripping hazards, and ensure proper lighting in the home.

Conclusion

At Swarnavihar Oldage Homes, we are dedicated to creating a supportive environment where senior citizens can thrive. Improving health in old age involves a holistic approach that encompasses physical, mental, and emotional well-being. By staying active, eating well, socializing, and prioritizing preventative care, seniors can lead fulfilling, healthy lives in their golden years.

What is Palliative Care?

Palliative consideration is a wide methodology pointed toward working on the personal satisfaction for people with difficult sicknesses, no matter what their stage or visualization. It centers around giving help from side effects, torment, and stress brought about by the ailment and its medicines.

Key Features of Palliative Care

  • Comprehensive Symptom Management: Addresses a scope of side effects, including agony, queasiness, and weariness, to further develop solace.
  • Supportive Care: Offers close to home and mental help to patients and their families.

When is Palliative Care Appropriate?

Palliative consideration is reasonable for people at any phase of a difficult sickness, whether it is constant, life-restricting, or possibly reparable. It is expected to be a supplement to other clinical medicines, intending to further develop the patient’s personal satisfaction.

What is Hospice Care?

Hospice care is a particular type of palliative consideration planned explicitly for people who are approaching the finish of life. It centers around giving solace and backing as opposed to trying to fix the sickness.

  • End-of-Life Focus: Stresses solace and personal satisfaction during the last phases of life.

title.rendered: Best Tips to Take Care of Dementia Patients

content.rendered:
Caring for someone with dementia requires understanding, patience, and specialized care strategies to manage the condition effectively. Whether you are a family caregiver or a professional, knowing the essentials about dementia, including its causes, symptoms, risk factors, and treatments, can make a significant difference in providing high-quality care. Here’s a comprehensive guide to help you navigate the complexities of caring for dementia patients.

Causes of Dementia Patients

Dementia is a term that describes a range of symptoms associated with a decline in cognitive function severe enough to interfere with daily life. The primary causes of dementia can vary, but some of the most common include:

  • Alzheimer’s Disease: The most common form of dementia, characterized by memory loss and cognitive decline due to brain cell damage.
  • Vascular Dementia: Caused by reduced blood flow to the brain, often resulting from strokes or other vascular conditions.
  • Lewy Body Dementia: Associated with abnormal protein deposits in the brain that affect movement, cognition, and sleep.
  • Frontotemporal Dementia: Involves progressive damage to the frontal and temporal lobes of the brain, affecting behavior and language.

Understanding the underlying cause of dementia helps in tailoring care plans and managing symptoms more effectively.

Signs and Symptoms of Dementia Patients

Recognizing the signs and symptoms of dementia is crucial for early intervention and effective management. Common symptoms include:

  • Memory Loss: Difficulty remembering recent events, conversations, or appointments.
  • Confusion: Disorientation about time, place, or identity of familiar people.
  • Difficulty with Communication: Trouble finding the right words or following conversations.
  • Changes in Mood and Behavior: Unpredictable mood swings, agitation, or withdrawal from social activities.
  • Impaired Judgment: Poor decision-making or difficulty managing finances and daily tasks.

Monitoring these symptoms can help in providing appropriate care and seeking professional help when necessary.

Risk Factors

Several risk factors can increase the likelihood of developing dementia. While some are non-modifiable, understanding these can help in taking preventive measures:

  • Age: The risk of dementia increases with age, particularly after 65.
  • Genetics: Family history of dementia can raise the risk, with specific genes linked to certain types of dementia.
  • Cardiovascular Health: Conditions like high blood pressure, diabetes, and high cholesterol can contribute to dementia risk.
  • Lifestyle Factors: Smoking, excessive alcohol consumption, and lack of physical activity can increase risk.
  • Head Injuries: A history of traumatic brain injury may be linked to a higher risk of dementia.

Addressing these risk factors through lifestyle changes and regular medical check-ups can help in reducing the risk.

Treatment of Dementia Patients

While there is currently no cure for dementia, several approaches can help manage symptoms and improve quality of life:

  • Medications: Certain medications can help manage symptoms and slow the progression of dementia. These include cholinesterase inhibitors (e.g., Donepezil) and memantine.
  • Cognitive Therapies: Cognitive stimulation therapy and memory training can support cognitive function and enhance daily living skills.
  • Behavioral Interventions: Techniques to manage behavioral symptoms and improve communication can be beneficial.
  • Supportive Care: Creating a safe and supportive environment, including routines and familiar surroundings, can help reduce confusion and agitation.

Medical Treatment of Dementia Patients

Medical treatment for dementia typically involves a multi-faceted approach:

  • Regular Medical Consultations: Ongoing care from a healthcare provider is essential for monitoring the condition and adjusting treatment plans as needed.
  • Specialist Care: Neurologists, geriatricians, and psychiatrists may be involved in providing specialized care and addressing specific symptoms.
  • Support Services: Access to support groups, counseling, and caregiver education can provide valuable resources and emotional support.

Caring for someone with dementia  involves understanding the complexities of the condition and implementing effective care strategies. By being informed about the causes, symptoms, risk factors, and treatment options, caregivers can provide compassionate and effective support, ultimately improving the quality of life for dementia patients. If you’re unsure about any aspect of care, consulting healthcare professionals and seeking guidance from dementia support organizations can offer additional help and resources.

title.rendered: 5 Things One Is Mostly Unaware Of Post-Operative Elderly Care

content.rendered:
Postoperative care is basically the care one receives after a surgical procedure. This kind of postoperative care, precisely, Post operative nursing care depends on the surgery type including your health history, pain management and wound care. Postoperative care done at Post operative care homes commences immediately after surgery is performed on the patients, lasting for the duration of hospital stay and continuing after the patient has been discharged from the hospital. As part of your postoperative care, your healthcare provider should make it a point to teach you about the potential side effects and procedural complications. Before surgery, ask your doctor what the Post operative nursing care, especially for the elderly, will involve. Your doctor may revise some of their instructions post-surgery based on how surgery is carried out and how well one is recovering from it.

Below are five basic pointers one is oblivious of when it comes to Post operative nursing care for the elderly carried out at Post operative care homes:

  1. Uncontrolled Pain-Whilst pain is commonplace post-surgery, this still needs to be taken care of in post-surgical care for the elderly. The reason is that in some elderly patients, painkillers or sedatives do not work any longer after surgical procedure. In no way the pain can be reduced by prescribed oral drugs, so the need to consult a doctor arises. However, problems with pain management tend to affect a patient’s ability to recover and recuperate, making recovery process a bit more tedious, lasting and uncomfortable than it actually requires to be. This is where the Post operative nursing care performed at Post operative care homes for the elderly comes into the picture!
  1. Confusion or Delirium-Coming out of anaesthesia is tough task indeed. Grogginess plagues a majority of those who went under the knife. But confusion or postoperative delirium treated at Post operative care homes, is different and is mostly seen amongst elderly people.

According to experts, more than 80% of elderly patients’ delirium go unaware and unnoticed. Here are the warning signs:

  • Distraction
  • Disorientation
  • Inability to utter certain words
  • Temporary memory loss
  • Hallucinations
  • Lack of awareness

If you notice any of the aforementioned symptoms amongst the aged ones, tell someone immediately for timely intervention.

  1. Increased Nausea-Medications and anaesthesia generate adverse effects on the patient’s body. If your loved ones or the elderly people have problem of this sort, it is quite normal. Nausea is not that alarming in itself. But if it persists for a longer period of time, it leads to dehydration. Give a call to professionals dealing with Post operative nursing care if vomiting and sickness do not subside of their own.
  1. Excessive Bruising-Post-surgery, it’s overwhelming to see the aftermath. To add to the woes, there is excessive bruising on most occasions. The reason is that there is every chance of blood being leaked out spreading to other places under the skin. It’s not uncommon to detect bruising around the surgery site. Don’t feel panicky if you can’t help yourself out. Get in touch with a professional working at Post operative care homes who can bail you out!
  1. Dehydration-In the midst of confusion, pain, lethargy, and tiredness, one may easily forget to drink water. It is very much common amongst elderly patients in surgical aftercare carried out at Post operative care homes. This explains why it’s crucial that someone must be there to remind them of hydrating themselves with water at regular intervals. Moreover, ice chips can go a long way. However, hydration aids in temperature spikes, nausea, and all kinds of post-op side-effects.

For most elderly patients, the road to recovery is a difficult one. As a caretaker, it’s quite a daunting task to think of the care your loved ones, especially, aged persons require-right from Postoperative nursing care to recovery in the future. title.rendered: Significant Role Of Communication In Dementia Care

content.rendered:
Dementia is a progressive ailment that, over a period of time, tends to affect a person’s ability to remember and recollect as well as understand basic everyday facts and events like names, dates and places. Dementia taken care of and treated in Dementia care, specifically, Dementia care homes in Pune, gradually affects the way a person usually communicates. Their ability to bring about practical, rational ideas and notions accompanied by subsequent reasoning power tend to change to a great extent. So, if you’re on the lookout for a person suffering from dementia, you may find that with the progression of illness, you need to go for initiating a discussion for getting the person communicate with you. With the onset of dementia attaining its peak, their capability to process information gets progressively and noticeably weaker with responses getting delayed every now and then.

Motivating someone with Dementia to Communicate:

Make an attempt to communicate with people suffering from dementia getting treated at Dementia care, in particular, dementia care homes in Pune, especially if you notice that they’re having far and fewer conversations. Communication aids in:

  • Speaking clearly and slowly, using short sentences.
  • Making eye contact with the person when they’re conversing or asking questions.
  • Providing them with time to respond and reciprocate, as they may feel pressurized if you attempt to speed up their answers.
  • Encouraging them to participate in communicating with others, whenever possible.
  • Letting them speak up their minds during discussions pertaining to their wellbeing or health concerns.
  • Trying not to patronize them, or ridiculing them about what they speak out.
  • Acknowledging what they’ve stated, even if they don’t answer to your query or speak out of context. Give the impression that you’ve heard them right thereby motivating them to say more about their answers.
  • Giving them smart and simple options-abstain from creating complicated or roundabout choices.
  • Using other means of communication like rephrasing questions as they’re unable to answer in the way they used to be.

Communication via Body Language & Physical Contact/Touch:

Communications is not just merely about talking or conversing. Gestures, movement and facial expressions all of these are capable of conveying meaning or help you get the messages across as part of dementia plan and program carried out in Dementia care, more so, at Dementia care homes in Pune. In fact, body language and physical touch/contact become important when speech seems to be a difficult proposition for a person suffering from dementia taken care of adeptly by Dementia care.

When someone has difficulty speaking up or understanding, make sure to:

  • Be patient and keep calm, resulting in the person communicate more freely, without any inhibitions or apprehensions.
  • Make your tone of voice positive, amicable and friendly, whenever possible.
  • Converse with them at respectable distance to avoid intimidating them-being in sync with them or even lower than they’re (for instance, if they’re sitting) can also help.
  • Pat on his/her back or hold the person’s hand whilst talking to them, reassuring them and making them feel closer-keep a tab on their body language, listening attentively to their thoughts or opinions to ascertain if they’re comfortable doing this.

In fact, good communication is an integral part of living well after diagnosis of dementia treated at Dementia care homes in Pune or anywhere in India. It helps people with dementia to keep a sense of self, sustain relationships and maintain their quality of life. Even as communication becomes more challenging, there’re lots of ways to communicate more meaningfully and effectively.

Listening to & Understanding someone with Dementia:

Communication is a two-way procedure. As a carer of someone who has been affected by dementia, you’ll probably have to learn to pay heed to what someone has to say. Moreover, you need to be much more aware of non-verbal messages like facial expressions and body languages, employing more physical contact such as reassuring pats on the arm, or smile and speaking as well.

Active listening helps in:

  • Using eye contact for looking at the person, and motivating them to cast his/her glance at you when either of you’re conversing.
  • Attempting not to interrupt them, even if you’re aware of what they’re talking about.
  • Stopping what you’re doing so that you can give full attention to the person whilst speaking.
  • Reducing distractions that act as a stumbling block in the way of communication like television viewing or radio playing too loudly. Do a reality check to see if it’s wise to indulge in such things or activities.
  • Repeating what you heard back to the person, asking him/her if it’s accurate or telling them to repeat those words.

Paralysis is the loss of muscle function in the body. Paralysis is sometimes temporary and, in a few cases, it is permanent. Paralysis is not limited to any particular part of the body, but most cases of paralysis are observed in limbs. Partial and complete paralysis can occur at any point in time. A patient suffering from paralysis is not inflicted by any pain upon occurrence.

A stroke is the most common underlying condition that triggers partial or complete paralysis in a patient. In partial paralysis, the patient is still in partial control of the affected muscle, incomplete paralysis, the patient has no control over the affected muscle tissue.

The most prominently known types of paralysis are:

Monoplegia:

Having trouble moving one limb is what monoplegia means. Sometimes, paralysis only happens in one arm. It can also affect some muscles in the same arm. Cerebral palsy often leads to loss of muscle function, also known as monoplegia.

Hemiplegia:

Hemiplegia is a kind of paralysis where people can’t move one side of their body. This usually only affects one arm and a leg, sometimes it’s also seen in the center of the body. Hemiparesis is a situation when someone doesn’t lose all use of their limbs, but how well they work is less strong and lasts shorter.

Hemiplegia happens because of harm to the spine or stroke, which affects how one side of your brain works.

The cure choice uses many blood thinners, pills to fight germs, operations and medicines for reducing swelling. Also included is exercises that help your body move better.

Paraplegia:

Paraplegia is a type of paralysis where the patient can’t move muscles from their belly down. In people with paralysis, the brain’s messages to lower body parts do not return upwards through the nerve hub. This poor talking with the brain, makes not only lose movement but also causes loss of feeling.

In partial paraplegia, the patient can still use one leg. In complete paraplegia they lose feeling and ability to use both legs. Big reasons for paraplegia are car crashes, getting hurt and falling.

Quadriplegia:

Quadriplegia is a type of paralysis where all four limbs can’t move. When this happens, the brain’s signals to areas below the neck do not go back. This makes holding and moving hands or legs difficult for patients. The spinal cord is in charge of sending and getting signals from the brain.

Locked-in Syndrome:

Locked-in Syndrome is the rarest and hardest type of not moving, where a person can’t control any muscles except those that make their eyes move.

Signs & Symptoms

Dementia affects each person in a different way, depending upon the impact of the disease and the person’s personality before becoming ill. The signs and symptoms linked to dementia can be understood in three stages.

Earlier stage: the early stage of dementia is often overlooked because the onset is gradual. Common symptoms include:

  • forgetfulness
  • losing track of the time
  • becoming lost in familiar places.

 

Moderate Stage: as dementia progresses to the middle stage, the signs and symptoms become clearer and more restricting. These include:

  • becoming forgetful of recent events and people’s names
  • becoming lost at home
  • having increasing difficulty with communication
  • needing help with personal care
  • experiencing behavior changes, including wandering and repeated questioning.

 

Late Stage: the late stage of dementia is one of near-total dependence and inactivity. Memory disturbances are serious and the physical signs and symptoms become more obvious. Symptoms include:

  • becoming unaware of the time and place
  • having difficulty recognizing relatives and friends
  • having an increasing need for assisted self-care
  • having difficulty walking
  • experiencing behavior changes that may escalate and include aggression.

Diagnosis

  • Doctors will check how well you think. There are many tests that check how well you think, like your memory and direction. They also measure your ability to reason and make decisions correctly. These tests can look at language skills too as well as paying attention carefully.

    Doctors check your memory, language skills, how you see things and pay attention. They look at problem-solving abilities and bodily movement too. This includes checking senses such as touch taste smell sound sense of stable body balance speed reaction reflexes etc. A physical test, blood tests and brain scans like a CT or MRI can help.

Types Of Dementia

  • Alzheimer’s disease: This is the main reason for dementia, found in 60 to 80 percent of cases. It happens because of certain alterations in the brain. The main sign is having trouble remembering things that happened recently like a talk you had just minutes or hours ago. Later in the disease, it gets hard to remember old memories too. Other issues like trouble with walking or talking, or changes in personality appear later on.

    Family background is the top risk factor. If a close family member gets Alzheimer’s disease, your chance of getting it too rises by 10 to 30 percent.

    Vascular dementia: About 10 percent of dementia cases happen because of strokes or problems with blood flow to the brain. Diabetes, high blood pressure and a lot of cholesterol are also things that can make you more likely to get heart disease. Symptoms change depending on which part of the brain and how big it is, that gets hit. The sickness moves in steps, so symptoms quickly get worse when someone has more strokes or small-strokes called “mini-strokes.”

    Lewy body dementia: Along with normal signs like forgetfulness, those who have this type of dementia might also face movement or balance issues such as stiffness and shaking. A lot of folks also feel different levels of wakefulness. This can involve feeling sleepy during the day, having trouble with thoughts or being lost in staring spells. They might also have troubles sleeping at night or could see things that aren’t really there like people, objects and shapes.

    Fronto-temporal dementia: This kind of forgetfulness usually brings about changes in personality and actions because it affects a part of the brain. People with this problem might feel ashamed or act badly in front of others. For example, a person who used to be careful might start saying mean things and stop doing their duties at home or work. There could also be issues with talking or grasping language.

    Mixed dementia: Sometimes, more than one kind of mental decline can be in the brain at once. This mostly happens to people who are 80 years old or older. For instance, a person might have Alzheimer’s disease and dementia caused by blood vessels. You can’t always tell if someone has both kinds of dementia because the signs from one might be stronger or could look like another type. The growth of illness may be quicker than with just one type of dementia.

    Reversible causes: People with dementia might have a fixable cause like medicine side effects, brain pressure increase, lack of vitamins or thyroid imbalance. Doctors should check for things that can be fixed in patients who might have memory problems.

Treatment:

The way to treat dementia depends on what’s causing it. There’s no cure for brain-wasting diseases like Alzheimer’s, though we have some drugs that can shield the mind or deal with problems such as sadness, sleep trouble, imagining things wrongly and fidgety behavior. Parkinson’s disease is one of these issues.

Doing regular exercise, eating good foods and having friends can help prevent long-term health problems. This may also lessen the chance of getting dementia.
